title: Why is it called a Grand Prix?
body: “Grand Prix” is French for “great prize.” The term dates back to early motor races in France and stuck as the official name for F1 championship rounds.

title: The chequered flag
body: The origin of the chequered flag is debated, but one popular theory ties it to horse racing and early US auto races where a checkered pattern was easy to spot at speed.

title: DRS explained simply
body: The Drag Reduction System opens a flap in the rear wing on designated straight zones when a driver is within one second of the car ahead, cutting drag and boosting top speed for overtaking.

title: Pole position origin
body: “Pole” comes from horse racing: the inside starting spot next to the rail (the pole). In F1 it means the front-row slot earned by the fastest qualifier.

title: Halo safety device
body: Introduced in 2018, the titanium halo protects the driver’s head. It has been credited with life-saving interventions in several major accidents since its debut.

title: Why teams change tyre compounds
body: Soft tyres grip more but degrade faster; hard tyres last longer with less peak grip. Strategy is a trade-off between pace, stint length, traffic, and weather.

title: Parc fermé rules
body: After qualifying, cars enter parc fermé — a locked-down state where major setup changes are banned until the race, keeping the grid fair.

title: Fastest lap point
body: In modern F1, the driver who sets the fastest race lap can earn a bonus point — but only if they also finish in the top 10.

title: Monaco’s unique challenge
body: The Monaco street circuit is slow by F1 standards but brutally punishing. Barriers are centimetres away, so mistakes are rarely forgiven and overtaking is extremely difficult.

title: What “undercut” means
body: An undercut is pitting earlier than a rival so you can use fresh tyres to jump them when they stop later. The opposite late-stop move is an overcut.

title: Blue flags
body: Blue flags warn a lapped car that faster traffic is approaching. Ignoring them repeatedly can earn a penalty for holding up race leaders.

title: Why engines are called power units
body: Modern F1 hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with energy recovery systems (ERS). Together they’re called a power unit, not just an engine.

title: Formation lap purpose
body: Before lights out, drivers complete a formation lap to warm tyres and brakes, check systems, and line up correctly on the grid.

title: Safety Car vs Virtual Safety Car
body: A Safety Car bunches the field behind a real car at reduced speed. A Virtual Safety Car forces all cars to slow by a set delta without lining up behind a lead car.

title: Team radio is delayed
body: Broadcast team radio is often on a short delay and selectively aired. Not every message fans hear is live, and not every message is shared.

title: Why rain changes everything
body: Wet races amplify driver skill and strategy. Intermediate and full-wet tyres, visibility spray, and rapidly evolving grip can scramble the entire order.

title: Constructor vs driver titles
body: F1 awards two championships: Drivers’ (individual points) and Constructors’ (combined points from both team cars). Teams fight hardest for the latter commercially.

title: The number 1 privilege
body: The reigning world champion may race with number 1 instead of their permanent number. Some champions keep their usual number for branding reasons.

title: Pit stop speed
body: Top teams routinely change four tyres in roughly two seconds. That choreography is one of the most practiced and measured operations in sport.

title: Why telemetry matters
body: Telemetry streams car data — speed, throttle, brake, gears, temps — to the garage. Engineers use it to coach drivers, manage tyres, and diagnose issues in real time.
